title: Chosun Expo — the front company behind the hacks
review_note: Condensed to under 6 minutes with own motion-graphics visuals (owner rules 2026-10-28). Facts unchanged from the verified version (DOJ press release, complaint affidavit via National Security Archive OCR copy, Dark Reading, SCMP, Wikipedia, NPR).

scenes.label: Coders for hire, on paper
scenes.narration: [dramatically] The hackers behind Sony and a bank heist were exposed by Gmail. [short pause] Not by a genius trick. By ordinary email accounts, the FBI says. [curious] On paper, their company was a normal software business. It was called Chosun Expo. [serious] But in 2018, the United States said it was a cover. [slowly] A cover for North Korea's hackers.

scenes.label: A coder named Park
scenes.narration: [calmly] Let's go back. Chosun Expo had offices in China and North Korea. It sold the work of North Korean coders to clients abroad. Some clients knew exactly who they were hiring, the FBI says. [short pause] One coder was Park Jin Hyok. He worked there from at least 2002. He looked like any other programmer. He even used his real name.

scenes.label: A day job in Dalian
scenes.narration: [softly] From 2011 to 2013, Park spent time in Dalian, a port city in northeast China. He worked on projects for paying clients. He used free Gmail accounts for company email. Many small businesses do that. [short pause] But the FBI says Chosun Expo had a second boss. It was tied to a hacking unit called Lab 110, part of North Korea's military intelligence.

visuals.text: open project; assign coder; deliver code; get paid

scenes.label: The hackers with a nickname
scenes.narration: [curious] Security experts chased a hacking group for years. They never learned the members' names. So they gave the group a nickname, the Lazarus Group. [serious] Prosecutors say Park was part of it. In 2014, a Hollywood comedy called The Interview was coming out. In the story, two Americans plot to kill Kim Jong Un. [short pause] North Korea called the movie an act of war.

visuals.text: Comedy: a plot to kill Kim
visuals.at: plot to kill Kim Jong Un

visuals.text: An act of war - North Korea's government

scenes.label: Bait for the actors
scenes.narration: [cautiously] In September 2014, strange Facebook messages appeared. One account used the names Watson Henny and John Mogabe. Another was Andoson David. They sent links to actors in The Interview. [short pause] The links were bait. Click one, and you could get malware. That's a program built to break into computers or damage them. [slowly] Someone was knocking on Sony's door.

visuals.text: link clicked; file opens; program runs

scenes.label: Hacked by GOP
scenes.narration: [dramatically] Then came November 21, 2014. Sony bosses got an email from someone calling himself Frank David. It demanded money. Three days later, Sony computers lit up with a message. It said, Hacked by GOP. That stands for Guardians of Peace. [breathless] Sony cut off about 8,000 computers to stop the damage. Private files spilled online. Even a new movie, Annie, leaked early.

scenes.label: $81 million walks out
scenes.narration: [serious] Hollywood was only the start. Next, the target was money. In February 2016, hackers broke into Bangladesh Bank, the country's central bank. They sent fake payment orders through SWIFT. That's the system banks use to send money across borders. [short pause] About $81 million got away. The FBI called it the biggest successful bank cyber-theft so far. [ominously] And the hackers wanted more.

scenes.label: Knocking at Lockheed Martin
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Prosecutors say the group tried to steal over $1 billion from banks. In 2016 and 2017, they sent spear-phishing emails to defense companies, including Lockheed Martin. That means fake emails made for one person, to trick them into clicking. Some mentioned a missile defense system called THAAD. [short pause] This time, the trick failed.

visuals.at: fake emails made for one person

scenes.label: WannaCry hits the world
scenes.narration: [urgently] In May 2017 came WannaCry. It was ransomware. That's a program that locks your files and demands money. It spread by itself, from computer to computer. Hundreds of thousands of machines were hit worldwide. [sad] In Britain, it hit the National Health Service. Thousands of hospital appointments were canceled. [pause] The FBI had been digging for years.

scenes.label: The clue in the inbox
scenes.narration: [curious] So how do you catch hackers from one of the most secretive countries on Earth? [short pause] The answer was email. Remember the free Gmail accounts Chosun Expo used? Some were in Park's real name. Agents found one was tied to a second Gmail account with a similar name. [serious] That second account was busy. It sent fake emails, studied targets, and researched hacking.

visuals.at: tied to a second Gmail account

visuals.text: send fake emails; study targets; research hacking

scenes.label: Who was Kim Hyon Woo?
scenes.narration: [serious] That second account used a name, Kim Hyon Woo. It was likely a fake name. Kim Hyon Woo accounts set up other email and social media accounts. Remember Andoson David, the Facebook bait account? [short pause] The FBI says it was set up with one of those same email addresses. [slowly] One thread now ran from the coder to the attacks.

visuals.text: Likely an alias or cover name

visuals.at: from the coder to the attacks

scenes.label: Too many fingerprints
scenes.narration: [calmly] Email wasn't the only clue. The same pieces of code showed up in different attacks. [short pause] Eric Chien, a Symantec security expert, said Park mixed his normal work with government work. And US search warrants could reach his American email accounts. [reflective] Priscilla Moriuchi said the case was built on all the mistakes he made.

visuals.text: Email was not the only clue
A lack of opsec - Eric Chien, Symantec

visuals.query: United States District Court Los Angeles

visuals.text: Built on all the mistakes he made - Priscilla Moriuchi

scenes.label: Charged, then denied
scenes.narration: [serious] On June 8, 2018, prosecutors filed a criminal complaint in Los Angeles. Then, on September 6, 2018, the charges went public. Park was charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and wire fraud. Wire fraud carries up to 20 years in prison. The US Treasury also put sanctions on Park and Chosun Expo. [surprised] North Korea's answer? It said Park Jin Hyok doesn't exist.

visuals.text: Park Jin Hyok doesn't exist - North Korea

scenes.label: Undone by an inbox
scenes.narration: [softly] As far as the public knows, Park Jin Hyok has never been arrested. The charges are still only accusations. [short pause] But the case put a real company behind years of attacks. [slowly] And what gave them away was the most ordinary thing in any office… an email account. [pause] If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

facts.claim: The complaint against Park Jin Hyok was filed June 8, 2018 in Los Angeles federal court and announced September 6, 2018.

Chosun Expo Joint Venture (Korea Expo Joint Venture) is described as a North Korean government front company with offices in China and the DPRK, affiliated with Lab 110, a component of DPRK military intelligence.
Affiant is FBI Special Agent Nathan P. Shields, Los Angeles Field Office; the affidavit's conclusion is at paragraph 171.
Chosun Expo stationed programmers abroad, including in Dalian, China, doing programming and IT projects for paying clients, some of whom knew they were hiring North Koreans.
Park worked for Chosun Expo from at least 2002, was in China for at least part of 2011–2013, and appears to have returned to North Korea by 2014; Chosun Expo accounts were in his true name.

In September 2014 a Facebook account using the names Watson Henny / John Mogabe posted malware links to actors in The Interview; an 'Andoson David' Facebook account, subscribed with the Kim Hyon Woo Gmail account, did the same.

A 'Frank David' email on November 21, 2014 demanded compensation from Sony; on November 24 workstations displayed 'Hacked by #GOP'; Sony disconnected 7,500 to 8,000 workstations; a pre-release copy of Annie was posted online.

About $81 million was stolen from Bangladesh Bank in February 2016 via fraudulent SWIFT messages; the affidavit calls it the largest successful cyber-theft from a financial institution to date; attempted losses 2015–2018 were well over $1 billion.
Spear-phishing of US defense contractors including Lockheed Martin in 2016–2017 was unsuccessful; a subject using a North Korean IP address researched and messaged Lockheed personnel.
The complaint alleges the same subjects authored WannaCry 2.0 (May 2017), which infected hundreds of thousands of computers, including in the Central District of California.
WannaCry hit the UK's NHS and thousands of appointments were canceled.

Chosun Expo used free email services for routine business; one Chosun Expo Gmail account was linked to a second with a similar handle used for spear-phishing, reconnaissance and hacking research; 'Kim Hyon Woo' was 'likely an alias or cover name'.
Investigators linked the attacks through email and social media accounts, aliases, malware collector accounts, common code libraries, proxy services and IP addresses.
A Brambul worm collector account was accessed from a North Korean IP address in 2017.

Eric Chien (Symantec) cited 'a lack of opsec' and said Park 'cross-contaminated' legitimate and government work; Priscilla Moriuchi (Recorded Future): investigators 'were able to build this case against him based on all the mistakes he made'; free US email exposed accounts to US search warrants.

Charges: conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse (max 5 years) and conspiracy to commit wire fraud (max 20 years); Treasury OFAC sanctioned Park and KEJV under E.O. 13722; Demers: 'The scale and scope of the cyber-crimes alleged by the Complaint is staggering'.
Park is on the FBI wanted list; North Korea denies that Park exists.
The company used free email services such as Gmail for routine business and for phishing; clues in Gmail helped investigators.
In June 2014 North Korea's government (via KCNA/foreign ministry) called The Interview, a comedy about a plot to kill Kim Jong Un, an 'act of war'.
Some spear-phishing emails to Lockheed Martin referenced THAAD, the missile defense system for which Lockheed is prime contractor; the attempts were not successful.
WannaCry spread itself from computer to computer (worm-like ransomware) and hit hundreds of thousands of computers, significantly impacting the UK's NHS.

seo.youtube_description:
How the FBI unmasked a North Korean hacker: the true story of Chosun Expo, the "software company" the US says was a cover for North Korea's hackers.
One coder for hire, Park Jin Hyok, is charged over the Sony Pictures hack, the $81 million Bangladesh Bank theft and WannaCry. What gave him away? Gmail.

On paper, Chosun Expo was a normal company. It had offices in China and North Korea and sold the work of North Korean programmers to paying clients. One of them, Park Jin Hyok, worked in Dalian, China, using his real name. But the FBI says the company was tied to Lab 110, a hacking unit in North Korea's military spy service, and to the hackers known as the Lazarus Group.

Prosecutors say the same group sent bait to actors in The Interview, wiped Sony computers in 2014, stole $81 million from Bangladesh Bank in 2016, went after Lockheed Martin and released WannaCry in 2017. The case cracked because of ordinary email accounts that linked Park's real name to a fake one, Kim Hyon Woo. He was charged in 2018 and sanctioned by the US Treasury. He has never been arrested, and the charges are still accusations.
